Well from the few photography classes I've had really old photos didn't have negatives, especially pinhole cameras. You can make a pinhole cameras with any size box and a bit of photoreactive paper, the kind that needs chemicals to develop, we made one in one of the classes and mine was made out of a octangular biscuit tin with some tape.

The picture that came out after about 30 seconds of exposure was pristine, even with my idiot handling and messy first time developing photos by hand mistakes. The picture was of the front of the uni, it was freaking beautiful in it's definition like a damn mirror.

Black and white though, considering it was our first time and the colour chemicals are just a ton of layers for a newbie.

Take that bare understanding and a fucking cake tin and apply a proper craftsman's effort at a time when this stuff was not only cutting edge but also normal enough that to stand out you had to be really good. Then add in they could use proper hand crafted equipment and set up the scene a little. That's why old photos look great, the best were hand crafted rectangles of soul. They were coveted as both an art piece and a pinnacle of human effort of the time, captured forever in a timeless slip of paper you could show your children a hundred years later.

All the boring, mundane or shitty photos were kept for a time but weren't considered important or nice enough to archive and faded or spoiled and were thrown out. We kept the spectacular ones and moved them along our timeline, updated them to reprints, video, digital and in some cases created acid carved tungsten carbide plates that can be kept flawlessly for the next 34,000,000 years in a sealed vault and still produce a perfect copy of that picture, when everyone who remembers the person who captured that moment are long, long gone.

We digitised photos of people living life, doing nothing amazing, just walking down the street. And then we inscribed their data onto a golden record along with instructions on how to decode them made in every way we could conceive of and put it on a satellite that has long since ran out of power on it's eternal trek out of our solar system, drifting endlessly out into the void with pictures encoded onto it, the subjects living life captured in that moment to live eternally in a golden immortality drifting through the depths of space, waiting for someone to find them and see them once more.
